summary.title: Writing a Linux Debugger: Part 8 - Stack Unwinding
summary.one_liner: You learn how to implement a backtrace command on x86_64 by walking the frame-pointer linked list and mapping return addresses to functions via DWARF info.
takeaways: A backtrace is the chain of function calls leading to the current program state, and it can be produced by walking saved frame pointers.
On x86_64, each stack frame stores the previous frame pointer, and the return address sits 8 bytes above it, so following this linked list unwinds the stack.
Return addresses are mapped to function names using DWARF info (get_function_from_pc), and the walk stops at main.
Compile with -fno-omit-frame-pointer so the compiler keeps the rbp-based frame layout this approach relies on.
The alternative is parsing .eh_frame or using libunwind, which the author considers more robust but more work.
summary.summary: This post is part 8 of a series on writing a Linux debugger in C++. It explains the purpose of a backtrace, then shows how to implement stack unwinding on x86_64 by assuming a standard frame layout and following the saved frame-pointer linked list. The author builds a print_backtrace function that prints each frame's function name and low PC using DWARF lookups, then exposes it as a backtrace command. It closes with testing advice and notes that the next post covers reading and writing variables.
